chapters.title: Settings reference
chapters.subtitle: The settings you actually touch
chapters.summary: A lookup table for the settings that change behaviour, security or deployment. Defaults are not repeated; this is the map of what to set and why.
chapters.quick_answer: Keep `SECRET_KEY`, `DEBUG`, `ALLOWED_HOSTS` and database credentials in the environment. Set `AUTH_USER_MODEL` before the first migration. Treat `SECURE_*`, `SESSION_COOKIE_*` and `CSRF_*` as one security group, not isolated knobs.

chapters.title: Model fields reference
chapters.subtitle: Fields, relations, options and Meta
chapters.summary: The field types and options that appear in real models, including database defaults, generated columns, PostgreSQL arrays and the Python/database distinction behind schema bugs.
chapters.quick_answer: Choose the narrowest field that fits. `null` is about the database; `blank` is about form validation. Use `DecimalField` for money, `DateTimeField` with `USE_TZ=True` for time, and a deliberate `on_delete` for every relation.

sections.title: Scalar fields
sections.body: The basic column types. Prefer `CharField` with a max length for short text and `TextField` for long text. Backend-specific fields are listed separately below so you do not copy PostgreSQL-only code into SQLite.

sections.title: Computed and backend-specific fields
sections.body:
`GeneratedField` moves a calculation into the database. Use it when the value must be correct for every writer, not only Django. The expression must be deterministic and use database-supported functions.

`ArrayField` and `HStoreField` are PostgreSQL-only. They are excellent when the data genuinely is a list or a string map; they are a poor substitute for a normalized relation when you need joins, constraints or portability.

`JSONField` is cross-database and useful for unstructured payloads, but it does not give you the indexing and validation of a real schema. Decide whether the shape is truly flexible before choosing it.

Migration warning: generated columns and backend-specific fields are schema features. Test them on the database you deploy to, not only on SQLite.
sections.note: Django 5.0+ has GeneratedField. ArrayField/HStoreField require PostgreSQL and the postgres extras.
sections.code:
from django.contrib.postgres.fields import ArrayField, HStoreField
from django.db import models

class OrderLine(models.Model):
    quantity = models.PositiveIntegerField(default=1)
    unit_price = models.DecimalField(max_digits=10, decimal_places=2)
    line_total = models.GeneratedField(
        expression=models.F("quantity") * models.F("unit_price"),
        output_field=models.DecimalField(max_digits=12, decimal_places=2),
        db_persist=True,
    )

class Product(models.Model):
    tags = ArrayField(models.CharField(max_length=40), default=list, blank=True)
    attributes = HStoreField(default=dict, blank=True)
    payload = models.JSONField(default=dict, blank=True)

sections.title: Relationship fields
sections.body: Relations are database constraints plus Python descriptors. Set `on_delete` and `related_name` deliberately.
sections.code:
author = models.ForeignKey(Author, on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name="posts")
profile = models.OneToOneField(User, on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name="profile")
tags = models.ManyToManyField(Tag, blank=True, related_name="posts")

chapters.title: QuerySet reference
chapters.subtitle: Methods, lookups, aggregation and optimization
chapters.summary: A fast lookup for the QuerySet methods and field lookups you use daily, plus the optimization methods that keep query counts predictable.
chapters.quick_answer: QuerySets are lazy. Use `filter`/`exclude`/`get`, `select_related` for FK/O2O, `prefetch_related` for M2M/reverse, `annotate` for per-row calculations and `aggregate` for one-row summaries. Call `.explain()` when a query is slow.

sections.title: Query methods
sections.body: These return QuerySets unless marked otherwise. Chain them before evaluation.

head: Method
Returns
Use for
rows: Rows as tuples or flat values

sections.title: Field lookups
sections.body: Append `__lookup` to a field. Related fields use `__` to join (`author__email`).

sections.title: Aggregation and expressions
sections.body: `aggregate()` returns one dict; `annotate()` adds a value per row.
sections.code:
from django.db.models import Avg, Count, F, Q, Sum

Post.objects.aggregate(total=Count("id"), avg_views=Avg("view_count"))
Author.objects.annotate(post_count=Count("posts"), total_views=Sum("posts__view_count"))
Post.objects.filter(Q(status="draft") | Q(published_at__isnull=True))
Post.objects.filter(view_count__gte=F("like_count"))
sections.note: `Count(..., distinct=True)` prevents double counting across multiple joins.

sections.title: Optimization methods
sections.body: These change the query shape, not the result. Measure before and after.

pitfalls: Calling `len()` on a QuerySet repeatedly.
Using `get()` where multiple rows are valid.
Forgetting `select_related` in a loop.
Filtering on an annotation alias in the same query on every backend.
Using `update()` and expecting signals/save().
checklist: Query count is known for the page.

chapters.title: Template reference
chapters.subtitle: Tags, filters, loaders and context
chapters.summary: The Django Template Language tags and filters you will actually use, plus the loader/context settings that affect every render.
chapters.quick_answer: Use `{% extends %}` for layout, `{% include %}` for fragments, `{% url %}` for links, `{% static %}` for assets and `{% csrf_token %}` in POST forms. Output is autoescaped; `|safe` is an explicit trust decision.

sections.title: Tags
sections.body: Tags control flow, inheritance, URLs and rendering.

sections.title: Filters
sections.body: Filters transform one value. They do not replace view logic.

sections.title: Loaders and context
sections.body: Templates are discovered through `DIRS` and app template dirs. The cached loader is enabled when `DEBUG=False`. Context processors add data to every render.

pitfalls: Using `|safe` on user input.
Hard-coding URLs instead of `{% url %}`.
Forgetting `{% csrf_token %}`.
Putting queries in template tags.
Assuming a context processor is free.

chapters.title: Deletion & constraints reference
chapters.subtitle: What happens to related rows, when deletion must fail, and how to keep invariants
chapters.summary: A decision-oriented reference for ForeignKey deletion, database constraints, soft deletes and the query cost of large cascades.
chapters.quick_answer: Choose `on_delete` from the lifetime of the child row, not from what makes the current error disappear. `CASCADE` owns, `PROTECT`/`RESTRICT` preserve, `SET_NULL`/`SET_DEFAULT`/`SET(callable)` detach. Put invariants in database constraints, not only in forms.

sections.title: on_delete, option by option
sections.body:
`on_delete` is required for `ForeignKey` and `OneToOneField`. It describes what Django should do to child rows when the parent is deleted. It is a data-lifetime decision, not a syntax decision.

| Option | Child after parent delete | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| `CASCADE` | Deleted too | The child is owned by the parent and has no independent meaning |
| `PROTECT` | Parent delete blocked with `ProtectedError` | The child is important enough that deletion must be explicit |
| `RESTRICT` | Parent delete blocked with `RestrictedError` | Like `PROTECT`, but a cascade from another path may still remove the child |
| `SET_NULL` | Foreign key set to `NULL` | The relation is optional and the child must survive; requires `null=True` |
| `SET_DEFAULT` | Foreign key set to its `default` | A known fallback row should own the child; requires a default |
| `SET(value_or_callable)` | Foreign key set to that value | A fallback needs a query or per-delete calculation; pass a callable |
| `DO_NOTHING` | Nothing | Only when a database trigger or external system owns the behaviour |

`RESTRICT` is often the better default for financial and audit data because it distinguishes "this row is required" from "this whole subtree is protected". `PROTECT` still has its place when every path should be blocked.

`on_delete` is Django-side behaviour. It is not automatically the database's `ON DELETE` clause. `db_constraint=False` removes the foreign-key constraint, so the database cannot protect you from an orphan; do not use it to silence a `ProtectedError` or a migration problem.

sections.title: PROTECT vs RESTRICT in practice
sections.body:
Both raise a `ProtectedError`-family exception and both stop the delete. The difference appears when the child is also reachable through a cascading path.

`PROTECT` blocks the delete no matter how the collector reached the child. `RESTRICT` allows the delete when the child would be removed by another cascade in the same operation. This is why `RESTRICT` is useful for a `Payment` that belongs to an `Invoice`: you cannot delete the invoice directly while payments remain, but if the customer is deleted and the invoice would cascade, the payment can go with it.

Catch the exception at the boundary and turn it into a useful response. Do not catch `Exception` and continue as if the delete succeeded.

`db_constraint=True` is the default and creates a real foreign-key constraint. Keep it. `db_constraint=False` is for legacy schemas or unusual migration ordering; it leaves referential integrity to application code, which means orphan rows are now your job.

sections.title: Soft delete without lying to the ORM
sections.body:
A soft delete keeps the row and marks it hidden. It is the right tool when history, audit or restore matters, and the wrong tool when the user expects the data to be gone.

The minimum design is a nullable `deleted_at` timestamp plus a manager/queryset that hides deleted rows by default. Add an explicit `all_objects` manager for admin and restore workflows. Every uniqueness constraint then needs a decision: does a deleted row still occupy the unique value?

Do not implement soft delete by overriding `delete()` and doing nothing. `QuerySet.delete()` does not call each object's `delete()` method, so the two paths diverge. Use an explicit `soft_delete()` service or manager method and a scheduled purge for data that must eventually disappear.

If a row must be truly erased for privacy, soft delete is not enough: build a hard-delete/export workflow and test it.

sections.title: Check, unique and conditional constraints
sections.body:
Constraints are promises the database keeps even when a script, bulk update or race bypasses forms.

- `UniqueConstraint(fields=[...])` enforces multi-column uniqueness. Use `condition=` for a partial unique rule, such as one active membership per user.
- `CheckConstraint(condition=Q(...))` enforces a row-level rule. In modern Django use `condition=`; older code may show `check=`.
- `violation_error_message` gives a useful message, but the database exception is still `IntegrityError`.
- `full_clean(validate_constraints=True)` validates constraints before a write, but `save()` still does not call it automatically.

Catch `IntegrityError` at the service or form boundary, inspect the constraint name if needed, and return a field error. Do not swallow it: a failed constraint means the write did not happen.

`UniqueConstraint` with `condition` requires database support for partial indexes. SQLite and PostgreSQL support it; check your target backend.

sections.title: Large deletes and cascade cost
sections.body:
A delete is not free. Django's collector walks relations, loads child rows, sends `pre_delete`/`post_delete` signals and then deletes. A large cascade can produce many queries and long transactions.

Practical rules:

- Delete in bounded batches for large tables, not one unbounded `QuerySet.delete()`.
- Know which relations cascade. A single `CASCADE` can turn one parent delete into thousands of child deletes.
- `PROTECT`/`RESTRICT` are cheap guards; use them before a destructive admin action.
- `QuerySet.delete()` does not call model `delete()` methods, but it does send delete signals. Do not put critical cleanup only in an overridden `delete()`.
- For audit-heavy tables, archive or soft-delete first and purge later with an explicit command.

Measure with query logging or `CaptureQueriesContext` before calling a cascade "fine".
sections.code:
from django.db import transaction

def purge_invoices(queryset, batch_size=500):
    total = 0
    while True:
        ids = list(queryset.values_list("pk", flat=True)[:batch_size])
        if not ids:
            break
        with transaction.atomic():
            deleted, _ = queryset.model.objects.filter(pk__in=ids).delete()
        total += deleted
    return total

# PROTECT/RESTRICT surface the problem before a large destructive batch.
# CASCADE may delete far more rows than the parent you selected.

pitfalls: Using `CASCADE` for a reference that must survive the parent.
Using `DO_NOTHING` without a database constraint or trigger.
Assuming `on_delete` is the same as the database `ON DELETE` action.
Using `db_constraint=False` to hide an integrity problem.
Adding a soft delete that breaks unique constraints or restore flows.
Catching `IntegrityError` without rolling back the transaction.
Running an unbounded cascade on a large production table.
checklist: Every relation has an `on_delete` chosen from data lifetime.
`db_constraint` remains enabled unless there is a documented reason.
Invariants are enforced by database constraints.
Large deletes are batched, measured and reversible.
Soft-deleted rows have an explicit restore and purge path.
